title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6489 – Reuters estimate
body: The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point.

title: Swiss inflation surprises higher in October but core prices offer some relief
body: Switzerland October CPI +1.5% vs +1.3% y/y expected Prior +1.0% Switzerland October core CPI +0.5% y/y Prior +0.5% Swiss headline annual inflation picks up at the start of the third quarter, rising to 1.5% from 1.0% previously. Much like elsewhere around the region, higher energy prices are the main culprit in continuing to feed through to consumer prices. As such, the inflation numbers may look to be heating up again at first glance. But in looking to core annual inflation, that remains unchanged at just 0.5%. That tells us that the broader inflation picture isn't quite as alarming as the headline reading might suggest. And for the SNB, that is the most crucial takeaway here. The central bank has been arguing for months that higher energy costs are largely responsible for the inflation pickup, with limited evidence of second-round effects spilling over to the wider economy. The latest figures we're seeing today doesn't really challenge that narrative as such. Naturally, headline inflation moving closer to the 2% mark does mean that policymakers won't be entirely comfortable if energy prices continue to stay elevated. That will especially be the case if there is more evidence of businesses eventually passing those higher costs on to consumers. But at least for now, the SNB still has room to sit comfortably on the sidelines and assess how persistent these inflation pressures might become. In other words, there's no reason to panic just yet.

title: US-Iran deal still out of reach despite fresh diplomatic hopes ahead of US midterms
body: And round and round we go. We started the week with renewed optimism that the US and Iran might finally be inching towards a diplomatic breakthrough. That led to oil prices tumbling on Monday as hopes of a potential deal gathered momentum. But fast forward to today, and we're pretty much back where we started. Anyone got a case of déjà vu? These have been the same sort of headlines that we have been dealing with for almost seven months now. The latest comments from a senior Iranian official to Reuters: Tehran's conditions must be met if the US wants the Strait of Hormuz reopened, with nuclear talks only possible afterwards Iran is prepared to respond forcefully to US strikes, both in the region and beyond Mediators are working hard to narrow gaps between Tehran and Washington Now, that is hardly the language of two sides getting ready to shake hands. The thing about all this is that the sticking point remains the same. Iran wants its demands addressed before reopening the Strait of Hormuz, while the US is not willing to agree to those terms. And despite the diplomatic exchanges, neither side appears ready to make the concessions needed to break the deadlock. For markets, it just exemplifies the narrative that the underlying geopolitical risks haven't gone anywhere. While Monday's selloff in the oil market may have shown how quickly traders were willing to price in a potential easing of tensions, the fact of the matter is the reality is not quite there yet.

title: RBA governor Bullock says it might be that this rate hike might not be enough
body: In case you missed it, the RBA raised its cash rate by 25 bps to 4.85% today in a less straightforward 6-3 vote. That takes the cash rate to the highest level in 18 years, with the central bank trying not to pre-commit to further tightening at this stage. So far, Bullock's tone in her press conference has been more neutral and even in the latest remarks here. She says that the rate hike today might not be the last one but in trying to make that judgment, "it is not as obvious" as compared to before. Adding that she doesn't know how high rates will need to go and that it is up to the market to interpret their messaging. Bullock continues to reaffirm that the central bank will stay on a data-dependent path in saying that "it is probably good to wait now and assess incoming data". Having said that, she continues to at least highlight that inflation remains a key concern heading into next year. But at least for now, the dissenting votes should tone down any overly hawkish expectations from the central bank for the immediate outlook. As mentioned here, markets were not pricing in strong odds of another rate hike to follow up the one today. And so, the RBA is reaffirming those expectations for the most part with their choice of language and communique this week.

title: Apple earnings beat fails to impress Wall Street as tech shares struggle ahead of US midterms
body: Another week and it's another big tech name that is finding out that even beating earnings estimates isn't good enough for Wall Street these days. Apple is that next big name to be struck down and the timing couldn't be worse for an already battered tech sector in markets. Apple reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $114.48 billion and earnings per share of $2.10, beating expectations of $113.39 billion and $1.99 respectively. Now, that sounds pretty decent no? Well, if only the market reaction shared that view. Apple shares instead are down 2% in after-hours trading as investors turned their attention to the less flattering details. As always, it is all about the guidance. Of note, Apple expects gross margins to decline to around 45-46% for the December quarter, down from 47.9%, as rising memory costs squeeze profitability. Meanwhile, services revenue growth is also projected at just 8-9% and that comes under expectations of around 10.7%. Besides that, there is also the fact that tariff refunds have flattered the latest quarterly results. So, there is good reason to question how much of the latest earnings strength will carry forward to the next one. In any case, we have seen over the past few weeks how Wall Street is turning more and more unforgiving when it comes to techn earnings especially. It's not enough to deliver good numbers anymore and disappointing outlooks are being punished hard.

title: Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) 25bp rate hike, as widely expected
body: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% on Tuesday, its fifth increase of 2026 and the highest level since 2008. The decision was far from unanimous, though: six board members voted to hike and three preferred to hold at 4.60%, a split that tempers the hawkish signal. The board said inflation remains elevated and broadly based, and that staff forecasts have been revised materially higher. Inflation is now expected to stay above 3% over the coming year and not to reach the top of the 2% to 3% target band until late 2027, about three quarters later than previously forecast. Higher fuel and commodity prices linked to the Middle East conflict are part of the story, but the RBA also judged domestic capacity pressures to be a little tighter than thought. It noted that firms are passing on costs and that some measures of inflation expectations have risen. AI-related investment is driving rapid price growth in technology goods. The board also acknowledged that its tightening is biting. The economy is slowing, house prices have fallen significantly and unemployment has risen, with the jobless rate now projected to climb further than expected in August. Weaker housing and consumer spending are expected to be partly offset by stronger business investment, including in data centres. Uncertainty remains high, with the RBA flagging scenarios in which inflation runs higher and growth weaker than forecast.

title: After the Binance hack, the simple security rule regulators keep coming back to, hot vs. cold wallets
body: South Korea's financial regulator wants local crypto exchanges to keep more customer assets in cold wallets, offline storage that hackers cannot reach over the internet. The push follows last week's $6.3 billion theft from Binance, which came entirely from the exchange's internet-connected hot wallets. Following the money: the playbook behind the $6.3bn Binance heist and a suspected $106 million theft The Financial Services Commission held an emergency meeting with major exchanges on 2 November. It reviewed how exchanges control access to their systems and approve withdrawals, and urged them to raise the share of assets held offline. It did not set a new legal ratio. The principle behind the request is simple: a hacker can only steal what is reachable online. Understanding the difference between hot and cold wallets explains why that matters, and why it is not a complete answer. What hot and cold wallets are A crypto wallet does not hold coins the way a purse holds cash. The coins live on the blockchain. What the wallet holds is the private key, a secret code that authorises spending. Whoever controls the key controls the coins. The difference between hot and cold is where that key sits. Hot wallet: the key is on a device or system connected to the internet. That makes it fast and convenient. An exchange can process thousands of withdrawals a day automatically, and an individual can trade or pay from a phone app in seconds.

title: Following the money: the playbook behind the $6.3bn Binance heist and a suspected $106 million theft
body: Two crypto thefts in less than a week show the same playbook. Stolen crypto moves along a predictable path, and the path is shaped by one fear above all others: being frozen. Knowing that path helps explain how much stolen money can be recovered, how much cannot, and why some of it may eventually reach the market. The big one is Binance. On 29 October, an attacker moved about $6.36 billion out of the exchange's hot wallets across ten blockchains, most of it in roughly 20 minutes, according to blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs. A hot wallet is an internet-connected wallet an exchange uses to process withdrawals. The FBI has attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking group, and it is the largest crypto theft on record. The smaller case is unconfirmed. Blockchain investigator ZachXBT said on Monday that an unnamed entity in the European Union may have lost more than $106 million from accounts at several exchanges on Sunday. Neither the victim nor the exchanges have been named, so treat it as a suspected theft. It is still useful, because the funds appear to have taken the same route. Step 1: Get out of stablecoins, fast Stablecoins such as Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC are the thief's biggest problem. Their issuers can freeze tokens sitting in a specific wallet, which turns stolen dollars into dead weight. That is exactly what happened at Binance.

title: US September factory orders +1.8% vs +1.2% expected
body: Prior factory orders +0.1% Factory orders excluding transportation +0.5% vs +0.3% prior Durable goods orders revisions +1.9% vs +1.8% prelim Durable goods excluding transportation revisions +0.5% vs +0.5% prelim Durable goods excluding defense +2.3% vs +2.2% prelim Nondefense capital goods orders excluding aircraft +0.6% vs +0.5% prelim This is a decent report and shows some momentum in factories but it's overshadowed by a jump in the JOLTS number released at the same time. US yields are moving higher in the aftermath of both and USD/JPY is at the highs of the day at 158.37. For background, the US Census Bureau's factory orders report, formally the full report on Manufacturers' Shipments, Inventories and Orders, is released monthly at 10 am ET, about five weeks after the reference month ends. It arrives roughly a week after the advance durable goods report and expands on it by adding nondurable goods. The headline figure is the monthly change in total new orders for manufactured goods. Nondurables include petroleum and coal products, chemicals, food, paper and plastics. For most nondurable industries, orders are essentially equal to shipments because products aren't built to order with a backlog. That means swings in oil and commodity prices feed straight into the nondurables figures, since refined petroleum products make up a large share. Markets also look at factory orders excluding transportation, which strips out the volatile aircraft and motor vehicle categories.

title: How markets price geopolitical risk: Why de-escalation headlines can trigger major market moves
body: Geopolitical events can have a significant impact on financial markets, especially when they threaten global energy supplies, trade routes or economic stability. Markets constantly assess the potential economic consequences, assign probabilities to different outcomes and adjust asset prices accordingly. This is why financial markets can rally sharply on the first signs of de-escalation, even when a conflict remains unresolved. Markets may move just based on expectations of a less negative scenario rathen than pricing in peace, for example. One of the most important concepts is that markets are forward-looking. Traders are constantly trying to anticipate what might happen over the next 6–12 months rather than caring about current conditions, because the present is already priced in. When geopolitical tensions escalate, markets begin to price in the potential economic consequences. These might include supply disruptions, higher energy prices, increased inflation, weaker economic growth and tighter financial conditions. These risks start to get incorporated into prices before the worst-case scenario actually materialises. For example, when tensions threaten the Strait of Hormuz, oil markets may start pricing in the possibility of supply disruptions even if no barrels have been physically removed from the market. The price increase reflects the additional risk of a future supply shock. The same mechanism works in reverse.

title: US midterms: Poll closing times today
body: Midterm election day continues in the United States without too much drama. All the talk of false flags and martial law on election day hasn't taken place and the polling disruptions have been minimal and certainly not widespread. Here's the schedule for when the polls close across the US. States that span two time zones close in stages, so the early calls in Indiana and Kentucky will only reflect partial results until the rest of each state closes an hour later. 6:00 pm: Indiana, Kentucky (eastern portions) 7:00 pm: Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont, Virginia, most of Florida and New Hampshire 7:30 pm: North Carolina, Ohio, West Virginia 8:00 pm: 21 states plus DC 9:00 pm: Arizona, Iowa, Minnesota, New York, Wisconsin and more 10:00 pm: Nevada, Montana, Utah 11:00 pm: California, Oregon, Washington, Idaho 12:00 am: Hawaii, Alaska The early East Coast closes will give the first read on the night. The main focus for markets is House and Senate control and what that means for the fiscal outlook. Many West Coast House races won't be decided for days, and California in particular counts slowly. So if the House is close, don't expect a clean answer before the European session. Prediction markets show Democrats with a 73% chance of controlling the Senate and a 93% chance of controlling the House. title: European Natural Gas Prices Fall Further
body: European natural gas prices dropped more than 3% on Tuesday to below €92/MWh, their lowest level in over a week, extending Monday's 8.7% slide. The pullback followed reports of progress toward a possible US–Iran diplomatic deal, which raised hopes of an end to the eight-month conflict and reduced the geopolitical risk premium that had pushed prices above €100/MWh last week for the first time since 2022. Nonetheless, structural supply concerns persist as colder weather drives up demand and storage levels lag behind official targets. Germany's gas reserves stood at just 61.05% of capacity on November 2, short of the government's 70% goal, while EU-wide inventories remained below 75%, the lowest level ever recorded for this point in the year. Forecasts point to further temperature declines across Northwest Europe this week, intensifying heating needs and reinforcing the region's reliance on additional LNG imports. title: NZ Q3 Unemployment rate 5.7% (expected 5.5%, prior 5.6%)
body: The miss on every major measure is likely to weigh on the New Zealand dollar and trim pricing for a December rate hike. The kiwi was already near a cycle low against the Australian dollar after last week's RBNZ hold, and the gap with a more hawkish RBA now looks set to widen. The weak jobs figures argue against tightening, but the RBNZ's hawks have focused on core inflation and fuel costs. A labour market miss alone may not settle the debate, so inflation expectations surveys later this month carry extra weight. Front-end swap rates are the market to watch for how far hike bets are pared. --- Banks called the peak in New Zealand unemployment, but the labour market went the other way, and the RBNZ's December hike now looks a harder sell. Summary: Unemployment rose to 5.7% in Q3 from 5.6%, against a Reuters poll forecast of 5.5% Employment fell 0.1% on the quarter, against expectations of a 0.4% gain, and Q2 growth was revised down to 0.3% The participation rate dropped to 70.4% from 70.6%, below the 70.7% forecast Private sector wages excluding overtime rose 0.4% on the quarter and 2.0% on the year, both slightly below forecasts The RBNZ held rates at 2.75% last week on a 4:3 vote, with the next decision on 9 December New Zealand holds a general election on Saturday New Zealand's unemployment rate rose to 5.7% in the third quarter, above expectations of 5.5%, as employment unexpectedly fell and wage growth slowed, data from Statistics New Zealand showed on Wednesday.

title: Nasdaq rebounds as chip stocks rally and Dow slips

title: AMD shares rise after hours as Q4 revenue outlook of $17bn tops forecasts on AI ramp
body: AMD's guide adds to a strong evening for the AI hardware trade, landing alongside Super Micro's beat and raised outlook, which may support chip and server names in the next session. The size of the fourth-quarter step-up will sharpen the comparison with Nvidia, since AMD is pitching Helios as a direct rack-scale rival. The slightly lower margin guide is unlikely to spoil the reaction on its own. It is still a reminder that volume growth in AI accelerators may come at some cost to profitability, which investors will weigh as the ramp scales. --- AMD beat modestly on the quarter but promised a big jump in the next one, betting that its Helios AI racks can turn into the growth engine investors have been waiting for. Summary: Q3 revenue was around $13.4bn, ahead of the roughly $13.1bn expected and up about 53% from a year earlier Adjusted EPS was about $2.10, against forecasts near $1.95 Adjusted operating margin was 29%, against expectations of 28%, with adjusted gross margin of 56% Q4 revenue guidance is around $17bn, above expectations of about $16.3bn Q4 adjusted gross margin guidance is 55%, slightly below the 55.5% expected AMD expects growth to accelerate as Helios and Venice production scales Shares rose in after-hours trade Advanced Micro Devices shares rose in after-hours trade after the chipmaker beat third-quarter forecasts and guided fourth-quarter revenue well above expectations.

title: Super Micro shares rise after hours as revenue nears $20bn and Q2 guidance tops forecasts
body: The after-hours gain extends a rally that began with last month's preliminary update, and the strong current-quarter guide gives the AI hardware trade another demand signal. In October, rival server makers Dell and HPE rallied in sympathy, so a similar read-through is possible in the next session. The full-year range is the weak point: it sits only modestly above expectations and could cap enthusiasm once investors work through the second-half arithmetic. The customer mix and margins remain the swing factors for whether the rally holds. --- Super Micro cleared even the higher bar it set for itself last month, though its full-year forecast quietly assumes the pace slows. Summary: Q1 revenue was around $19.9bn, against expectations of about $16bn and above the company's own preliminary range of $18.5bn to $19.5bn Adjusted EPS was roughly $1.80, ahead of forecasts near $1.20 Q2 revenue guidance is $19.5bn to $21.5bn, above the roughly $18bn expected Q2 adjusted EPS guidance is $1.66 to $1.90, against forecasts near $1.14 Full-year revenue guidance is $72bn to $78bn, broadly in line with expectations around $73bn Shares rose in after-hours trade Super Micro Computer shares rose in after-hours trade after the AI server maker reported fiscal first-quarter revenue of nearly $20bn. It also guided the current quarter higher still, extending the run of growth it previewed in a surprise update last month.

title: Two reasons why the US could attack Iran as soon as tomorrow
body: Oil has been falling this week but there's a fair argument that Trump could be attempting to send false signals in order to lower oil prices ahead of the vote. Behind the scenes, the US military has been angling to be in a position to attack immediately after the midterms. The New York Times cites US officials who say the US military could resume major combat operations against Iran as early as Wednesday. There are two reasons they US could launch the type of short and intense campaign Trump has teased. The first is that there are currently three US aircraft carriers in the region but one must return home in early November. USS George H.W. Bush— Already operating in the region. USS George Washington — Redeployed from the Pacific to the Middle East. USS Theodore Roosevelt — Deployed from San Diego in late September to reinforce U.S. forces. The USS George Washington is likely the one that needs to leave, returning ot its normal operating area near Japan. Secondly, early November is also a period of moonless nights and that's the darkness the US military generally prefers for its attacks, the report says. The NYT writes: U.S. Central Command has a plan to strike Iran beginning as early as Wednesday, after the U.S. midterm elections and when three aircraft carriers are in the region, according to U.S. officials. The ideal conditions for the type of campaign the military has laid out will last only a short time.

title: Booking Holdings shares slide as Q3 revenue misses despite earnings and bookings beat
body: The after-hours selling suggests investors care more about how much revenue Booking earns from its bookings than about volume. Strong gross bookings did not make up for the shortfall. The miss lands on a stock already down about 30% this year, which leaves little room for disappointment and could weigh on online travel peers in early trade. Oil is part of the backdrop: the company has linked higher flight prices and weaker long-haul demand to the Middle East conflict, so energy-driven airfare costs remain a risk to travel revenue. --- Booking's customers booked more travel than expected, but less of it turned into revenue, and that gap is what investors sold. Summary: Q3 revenue was around $8.9bn, short of expectations near $9.6bn Adjusted EPS was about $4.70, ahead of forecasts near $4.50 Gross bookings were roughly $54.5bn, above estimates of about $52.7bn Shares fell in after-hours trade Management had guided Q3 revenue growth of 4% to 6%, citing Middle East conflict effects on flights and long-haul travel Per-share figures reflect April's 25-for-1 stock split Booking Holdings shares fell in after-hours trade after the online travel group reported third-quarter revenue well short of expectations, overshadowing a beat on both adjusted earnings and gross bookings. According to the company's earnings release, revenue came in at around $8.9bn, against analyst expectations of about $9.6bn. Adjusted earnings per share were roughly $4.70, ahead of forecasts near $4.50.

body: The RatingDog PMI data follows official and their manufacturing PMIs earlier this week: details on these in the wrap for Monday, investingLive Asia-Pacific market news: Oil eases on Doha talks The NZ Q3 labour market data is due at 10:45am New Zealand time. What's expected Forecasts range from 5.4% to 5.6%. The June quarter's 5.6% was the highest since September 2015. Westpac expects employment to rise 0.5% and the rate to slip to 5.5%. ANZ expects employment up 0.3% and the rate unchanged at 5.6%. ANZ's flat call rests on a rise in labour force participation absorbing the job gains. The RBNZ's September forecast was 5.5%. Wage growth is expected to stay modest. Private-sector labour cost growth is forecast at around 2.1%, which economists describe as near a four-year low. RBNZ implications The RBNZ surprised markets on October 28 by holding the OCR at 2.75% on a 4:3 vote, when a 25bp hike had been almost fully priced. The majority pointed to softer than expected Q3 inflation, stable inflation expectations and subdued wage growth. That makes today's wage figures especially relevant. Westpac still expects a hike on December 9 but says it is not a done deal, and lists today's data as the first key input. ANZ also still forecasts a December move.
